name: Customer follow-up
headline: Know who is waiting and what happens next.
when: At the start of the day and after each customer contact.
owner: One named office contact keeps the record current. The estimator or project lead makes scope, price, and scheduling decisions.
steps: Capture the request once. Link to the original message or the record you already use.
Give every open item a person, a specific next action, and an agreed follow-up date. Waiting for a customer still needs a next check-in.
Review overdue and due-today items first. If a date slips, record why and agree the new date instead of silently moving it.
After contact, record what happened and set the next step. Close only when the outcome or accepted handoff is recorded.
done: Every open request has an owner, an action, and a due date. Closed requests have a recorded outcome or a handoff accepted by the next person.
exception: If a request raises an urgent concern, use the company’s agreed escalation process immediately. This sheet does not send alerts or replace that process.
examples: Ask customer for the floor plan
Confirm whether the added room changes the scope
Customer asked to add one room; no new price promised
Project lead accepted the handoff on Nov 2
Accepted by Casey; next action recorded in project EX-103
preview: Ask the customer for the floor plan.
Record the attempt and agree the next check-in.
fields: Reference: use the existing inquiry or job ID so related records can be found. Request: one sentence describing the customer’s need.
Owner: a person who has accepted the next action. Next action: a verb and a result, such as ‘Ask for the floor plan’ rather than ‘Follow up’.
Due: the next internal action date, not a customer appointment or promised completion date. Enter a real spreadsheet date.
Status: New, Waiting for customer, Waiting for team, or Closed. Last update: the latest contact, result, or reason a date changed.
Source or outcome: link to the source record while open. On closing, record the result or who accepted the handoff and where the next action is tracked.

name: Website updates
headline: Keep the wording, approval, and final check together.
when: Whenever a website correction or new page is proposed.
owner: The person making the edit owns the task through the final check. A named company approver confirms the facts and wording.
steps: Record the page, the proposed change, and the source needed to confirm it.
Prepare the exact wording or page preview. Record the approver and the dated approval for that version.
After approval, save the previous version and publish using the agreed account and access.
Check the published page on a phone and desktop. Test affected links and record the URL, check date, and any remaining action.
done: The approved version is live, the affected content and links have been checked, and the result is recorded. Approval alone does not finish the task.
exception: If the fact is unconfirmed, keep the change in ‘Needs facts’. If a live check fails, record the problem and restore the previous version or arrange a correction with the site owner.
examples: Explain what to send for a build-out inquiry
Confirm which plans the estimator needs
Ask estimator for the minimum useful project details
Add a project city or ZIP field
Draft form and proposed field labels
Review wording and confirm where submissions should arrive
Save the previous version, publish, then check the live page
preview: Add a city or ZIP field to the contact form.
Confirm the label and where submissions should arrive.
Approved, published, and checked on phone and desktop.
fields: Page: the exact page or profile being changed. Proposed change: link to the draft and name its version when wording changes.
Fact or source to confirm: the document or person supporting the claim. Leave unknown facts unresolved rather than guessing.
Approver and Approval date: the person and date attached to that version’s approval. Blank dates mean approval has not been recorded.
Owner and Due: the editor and next internal delivery date. Status: move from Needs facts through review, approval, publishing, and checking.
Published check record: the final URL, reviewer, check date, and result. Next action: the step still needed; a ‘Checked’ item has no unresolved correction.

name: Weekly handoff
headline: Bring the owner a short list of decisions.
when: Before the agreed weekly check-in and before someone covers the work.
owner: The person maintaining the website and follow-ups prepares the update. The manager resolves priorities and assigns decisions.
steps: Review the existing follow-up and website records. Link to them instead of copying every detail.
List what finished, what is waiting, and the exact decision needed. Include the effect of leaving a decision open.
Agree an owner and date for each next step. Write the decision back into the original record after the meeting.
For time away, name the cover person and confirm they can access the records and understand the next actions.
done: Each open decision has a person and a date. Decisions are written back into the source records, and any cover person has accepted the handoff.
exception: A time-sensitive issue goes to the responsible person when it arises. It does not wait for the weekly meeting.
examples: Project lead accepted the request; source record updated
Confirm who will review the added room; customer reply is waiting
Approve the proposed location field and submission destination
preview: A project lead accepted the site-visit handoff.
Who will review the added room in estimate EX-102?
The customer’s reply is waiting on that scope decision.
Record the decision in EX-102 and set the next action.
fields: Week of: the Monday starting the review week. Type: Finished, Decision needed, Next priority, or Cover handoff.
Item or reference: a source record ID or link. Update or decision needed: the result, exact question, or handoff to accept.
Owner: the person responsible for the next decision or action. Due: when it is needed; leave blank only for completed items.
Status: Open, Decision recorded, Handoff accepted, or Done. Recording a decision also means updating the original task.
Keep the update short. Bring unresolved decisions and significant changes rather than every routine contact.
